Issued at 347 PM CDT Sat Sep 26 2026

SYNOPSIS:

A cutoff low was centered over New England this afternoon with 
a southwest to northeast oriented upper-level ridge over the 
Great Lakes. An upper-level trough was located over the Pacific 
Northwest. A shortwave trough axis stretched from the Dakotas 
southeastward into northern Iowa as of 20Z. Height falls and 
isentropic lift to the northeast of the trough axis supported a 
broad area of light rain from the Ontario/Manitoba border 
southward across Minnesota into northeast Iowa. A southerly 
25-40 knot low-level jet was focused over the northern half of 
Minnesota supporting large scale ascent. Regional radar mosaic 
and GOES-East infrared satellite imagery revealed a tightly 
wound mesoscale low centered between St. Cloud and Alexandria.

LATE THIS AFTERNOON THROUGH SUNDAY:

The meso low will continue to propagate northward across 
central and north-central Minnesota through this evening. 
Subsidence on the right-rear flank of the meso low was eroding 
the precipitation over south-central and southeast Minnesota. 
Meanwhile farther west in the Red River Valley, scattered 
showers developed over the past hour. Look for the stratiform 
rain area to gradually shift eastward through this evening. 
High-res model guidance supports showers redeveloping west and 
south of the stratiform rain through this evening, similar to 
the progression we saw on Thursday. Locally enhanced rainfall is
likely in the vicinity of the meso low. Rain amounts of 
0.25-0.50 inches remain likely over central and north-central 
Minnesota with lower totals farther east where dry air was 
located.

Showers will gradually diminish overnight and Sunday morning as
the shortwave trough departs the Northland. Skies are expected 
to clear gradually through the day from west to east. 
Temperatures will trend warmer in central and north-central 
Minnesota with highs in the upper 60s to low 70s. Farther east 
temperatures will reach the low to middle 60s where clouds will 
remain the longest. Shower chances dwindle by late morning and a
few sprinkles may persist into the afternoon over northwest 
Wisconsin and the eastern portion of the Arrowhead.

MONDAY AND TUESDAY:

The blocking cutoff low will persist into the first half of 
next week while the western trough digs into the Rockies and 
Plains. Moisture return ahead of the trough will be enhanced by 
the flow around Hurricanes Polo and Odalys. Tropical moisture 
will stream northeastward around the southern periphery of the 
Rockies and into the Plains and western Great Lakes. A broad 
area of rain is forecast to develop over the Plains Monday and 
spread into the Northland Monday night and Tuesday. The timing 
of two distinct surges of tropical moisture remain a core 
concern with the forecast. As we noted yesterday and Thursday, 
the Northland appears to be positioned between the best moisture
advection on Monday and the moisture advection on Tuesday. 
While most of the Northland has a good chance of seeing 
measurable rainfall, the greatest rain amounts will once again 
be focused over central and north-central Minnesota. More 
substantial precipitation is forecast over the eastern Dakotas 
Monday and portions of Iowa and Wisconsin on Tuesday.

Winds over the southwest arm of Lake Superior will turn 
northeasterly again on Monday and may become strong enough to 
pose a risk of rip currents. The orientation and magnitude of 
the surface pressure gradient is less favorable than what we see
today, so confidence in hazardous swimming conditions is not as
high as we saw today.

LATE NEXT WEEK:

Near to above normal temperatures persist Wednesday with zonal 
flow expected aloft. A cold front is forecast to move 
southeastward across the region Thursday and Friday which will 
bring a temporary pause to the above normal conditions. 
Widespread frost is possible Friday night and next Saturday 
night. There will be a chance of rain with the frontal passage 
although better chances will be found to our south over the 
Middle Mississippi River Valley.
